Leaflet is an open-source JavaScript library for interactive maps. Static maps are well-suited for conveying a single, pre-specified message. Interactive maps serve a different purpose: they let the reader (or analyst) **explore** the data themselves — zooming in, clicking for attributes, toggling layers, and adjusting the view dynamically. The R package `leaflet` provides a bridge between the spatial objects we already work with (`sf`, `terra`) and a fully interactive, browser-based map widget. Key use cases: - Embedding interactive dashboards inside **R Markdown / Quarto** documents - Combining with `shiny` to build fully interactive web applications *(not covered in this course)* # `leaflet` ## Main References - Agafonkin, V. (2023). *Leaflet for R*. - Lovelace, R., Nowosad, J. & Muenchow, J. (2019). *Geocomputation with R*. Chapman and Hall/CRC. - Pebesma, E. (2018). Simple features for R. *The R Journal* 10(1), 439–446. ## The Map Widget The entry point to `leaflet` is the **map widget**: an interactive map window rendered in the browser (or in the RStudio Viewer pane). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(leaflet) # Create an empty widget m <- leaflet() m # print / render ``` ::: The widget is built up by **piping layers** with `%>%`, exactly like adding `geom_*` layers in `ggplot2`. The important constraint is that all spatial data must use the **standard geographic CRS EPSG:4326** (WGS 84 longitude/latitude). --- ## Adding Point Data ### `addCircles()` Renders each point as a scalable circle. Useful when you want the symbol size to reflect distance on the ground (radius in metres). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(leaflet) library(spData) m <- leaflet() %>% addCircles(data = nz_height) m ``` ::: ### `addMarkers()` Renders each point as the classic pin/teardrop marker icon. Useful for discrete locations where you plan to attach popups or labels. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m <- leaflet() %>% addMarkers(data = nz_height) m ``` ::: --- ## Adding Polygon and Line Data ### `addPolygons()` Adds `sf` POLYGON (or MULTIPOLYGON) objects as filled, bordered shapes. Layers are added in the order they appear in the pipe — put polygons before points so the points are drawn on top. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m <- leaflet() %>% addPolygons(data = nz) %>% # polygon layer (underneath) addMarkers(data = nz_height) # point layer (on top) m ``` ::: ### `addPolylines()` The equivalent function for `sf` LINESTRING geometries (roads, rivers, borders). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Generic pattern: m <- leaflet() %>% addPolylines(data = my_lines_sf) ``` ::: --- ## Adding a Background Map Tile Without a background, the widget renders on a plain grey canvas. Add a tile layer with `addTiles()` (uses OpenStreetMap by default) to give the map geographic context. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m <- leaflet() %>% addTiles() %>% # OSM background addMarkers(data = nz_height) m ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note} The default `addTiles()` pulls tiles from **OpenStreetMap** (CC-BY-SA licence). This is suitable for exploratory work. For publications, check the provider's licence terms. ::: --- ## Controlling the Initial View: `setView()` By default, `leaflet` zooms to the bounding box of the data. You can override this with `setView()`, specifying a centre coordinate and an integer zoom level from 0 (whole world) to 18 (building level). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m <- leaflet() %>% setView( lng = 170.141717, # Mt. Cook, New Zealand lat = -43.595296, zoom = 3 # country level ) %>% addTiles() %>% addMarkers(data = nz_height) m ``` ::: Increasing the zoom level: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m <- leaflet() %>% setView( lng = 170.141717, lat = -43.595296, zoom = 13 # street / valley level ) %>% addTiles() %>% addMarkers(data = nz_height) m ``` ::: | Zoom level | Approximate scale | |-----------|------------------| | 0–2 | World / continent | | 3–6 | Country | | 7–10 | Region / state | | 11–13 | City / town | | 14–16 | Neighbourhood | | 17–18 | Building level | --- ## Changing the Background Provider `addTiles()` defaults to OpenStreetMap, but many alternative tile sets are available via `addProviderTiles()`. The full list is accessible at `leaflet::providers`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m <- leaflet() %>% addProviderTiles( provider = providers$CartoDB.Positron # clean, minimal basemap ) %>% addMarkers(data = nz_height) m ``` ::: Other commonly used providers include `providers$Esri.WorldImagery` (satellite), `providers$Stamen.Toner` (high-contrast), and `providers$Esri.NatGeoWorldMap` (National Geographic style). --- ## Popups and Labels Both popups and labels attach attribute information to point markers. The key practical constraint: the value must be coercible to a **character** string (use `as.character()` if needed). The formula notation `~column_name` references columns of the data object passed to `data =`. ### Popups — click to reveal Popups appear **on click**. They are appropriate for detailed information that would clutter the map if always visible. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m <- leaflet() %>% addTiles() %>% addMarkers( data = nz_height, popup = ~elevation # must be character; numeric works here via coercion ) m ``` ::: ### Labels — hover to reveal Labels appear **on hover** (mouse-over). They are better for quick, at-a-glance information when browsing the map. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m <- leaflet() %>% addTiles() %>% addMarkers( data = nz_height, label = ~elevation ) m ``` ::: ::: {.callout-tip} To show richer HTML content in a popup (e.g. bold text, multiple fields), build the string with `paste()` or `glue()` and wrap it in `htmltools::HTML()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} popup_text <- paste0( "Elevation: ", nz_height$elevation, " m" ) m <- leaflet() %>% addTiles() %>% addMarkers(data = nz_height, popup = popup_text) ``` ::: ::: --- ## Adding Raster Data: `addRasterImage()` Continuous raster layers (elevation, NDVI, temperature, etc.) can be overlaid on a `leaflet` map with `addRasterImage()`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # r.elev must be a raster::raster() object (not a terra SpatRaster directly) m <- leaflet() %>% addTiles() %>% addRasterImage(r.elev) %>% addCircles(data = nz_height) m ``` ::: ::: {.callout-warning} ### Two important caveats for rasters 1. **Extent**: `leaflet` uses EPSG:4326 (geographic coordinates). If your raster is in a projected CRS, reproject it first with `terra::project(r, "EPSG:4326")` or the `raster` package equivalent. 2. **Object class**: `addRasterImage()` requires a `raster::raster()` object, **not** a `terra::SpatRaster`. Convert with: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} r_leaflet <- raster::raster(r_terra) ``` ::: For large rasters the file size rendered in the browser can become very large. Consider aggregating or clipping to the area of interest first. ::: --- # Spatial Data via APIs ## What Is an API? An **API (Application Programming Interface)** is a standardised communication channel that allows software systems to exchange data. Web APIs expose data over HTTP: you construct a URL with parameters, send a GET request, and receive a structured response (typically JSON or XML). For geospatial work, APIs are valuable because they let you: - **Geocode** addresses or place names → coordinates - **Retrieve boundaries** for administrative units on demand - **Query remote datasets** (land cover, population, climate) without downloading entire files ## Geocoding with `https://geocode.maps.co/` A **geocoding** API converts a text string (address, place name) into a latitude/longitude coordinate. The `geocode.maps.co` service offers a free tier that is sufficient for classroom use (registration required for an API key). ### Manual vs. Automated You could geocode by hand: visit the website, type "Barcelona UPF", click Find, and record the coordinates (41.387917, 2.169919). But if you need coordinates for dozens or hundreds of places, manual entry is impractical. An API call automates this: you pass the query string programmatically and parse the response in R. ### R Implementation with `httr` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(httr) library(sf) # Build the request URL # Note: spaces in the query must be encoded as "%20" query <- "UPF%20Barcelona" api_key <- "YOUR_API_KEY_HERE" url <- paste0( "https://geocode.maps.co/search?q=", query, "&api_key=", api_key ) # Send GET request and parse JSON response response <- GET(url) result <- content(response, as = "parsed") # Extract coordinates from first result lat <- as.numeric(result[[1]]$lat) lon <- as.numeric(result[[1]]$lon) # Convert to sf POINT object (EPSG:4326) upf_sf <- st_as_sf( data.frame(name = "UPF Barcelona", lon = lon, lat = lat), coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326 ) ``` ::: ### Combining API Results with Existing `sf` Objects Once geocoded results are stored as `sf` objects, they integrate seamlessly with everything else in the spatial workflow: spatial joins, buffers, visualisation with `ggplot2` or `leaflet`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Example: plot UPF location against Barcelona district boundaries library(ggplot2) ggplot() + geom_sf(data = bcn_boundaries) + # pre-loaded district polygons geom_sf(data = upf_sf, colour = "red", size = 3) + theme_minimal() ``` ::: --- # Summary: `leaflet` Function Reference | Task | Function | Key arguments | |------|----------|---------------| | Create widget | `leaflet()` | `options = leafletOptions(...)` | | OSM background | `addTiles()` | — | | Custom background | `addProviderTiles()` | `provider = providers$...` | | Set initial view | `setView()` | `lng`, `lat`, `zoom` | | Add point markers | `addMarkers()` | `data`, `popup`, `label` | | Add point circles | `addCircles()` | `data`, `radius`, `color` | | Add polygons | `addPolygons()` | `data`, `fillColor`, `weight` | | Add lines | `addPolylines()` | `data`, `color`, `weight` | | Add raster | `addRasterImage()` | `x` (raster object), `colors`, `opacity` | ::: {.callout-tip} ### Pipe order matters `leaflet` layers are drawn in the order they appear in the pipe. Put background tiles first, then polygon layers, then point layers — so that points are always rendered on top of polygons and both are on top of the basemap. ::: --- # Hands-On Exercises ## Exercise 1: Reproduce a Static Map as a `leaflet` Widget Take the multi-layer `sf` plot from Lecture 02 (which showed POINT, LINESTRING, and POLYGON objects together) and recreate it as an interactive `leaflet` widget. - Use the same `sf` objects as inputs - Add each geometry type as a separate layer - Use `addTiles()` for the background - Ensure the projection is EPSG:4326 ## Exercise 2: Ohio House Sales Plot a subsample of the `spData::house` dataset (house sales in Ohio) as a `leaflet` widget. - Use `dplyr::sample_n(20)` to draw a manageable subsample (the full dataset is very large) - Reproject to EPSG:4326 with `sf::st_transform(house, 4326)` before passing to `leaflet` - Display the **sale price** as a hover label (`label = ~price`) - Use a custom background tile (e.g. `providers$Esri.NatGeoWorldMap`) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(leaflet) library(spData) library(dplyr) library(sf) house_sample <- house %>% sample_n(20) %>% st_transform(4326) leaflet() %>% addProviderTiles(providers$Esri.NatGeoWorldMap) %>% addMarkers( data = house_sample, label = ~as.character(price) ) ``` ::: ## Exercise 3: API Geocoding — UPF Barcelona Use the `geocode.maps.co` API to locate all UPF Barcelona campuses and cafeterias. 1. Construct the query URL for `"UPF%20Barcelona"` and send a GET request with `httr::GET()` 2. Parse the JSON response and extract all returned locations (name, lat, lon) 3. Convert results to an `sf` POINT object (EPSG:4326) 4. Download Barcelona district boundaries (available at the link in the slides) 5. Plot both layers together with `ggplot2` **Extension**: use `sf::st_buffer()` to create a 1.5 km buffer around all UPF locations, intersect with the district boundaries, and visualise only the districts that fall within that buffer. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Buffer and spatial filter (extension) library(sf) upf_buffer <- st_buffer( st_transform(upf_sf, 25831), # project to metres (ETRS89 UTM zone 31N) dist = 1500 # 1.5 km ) %>% st_transform(4326) # back to geographic for leaflet bcn_within <- bcn_boundaries[ lengths(st_intersects(bcn_boundaries, upf_buffer)) > 0, ] ``` ::: --- ## References - Agafonkin, V. (2023). *Leaflet for R*. - Lovelace, R., Nowosad, J. & Muenchow, J. (2019). *Geocomputation with R*. Chapman and Hall/CRC. - Pebesma, E. (2018). Simple features for R: Standardized support for spatial vector data. *The R Journal* 10(1), 439–446. - Wickham, H. & Grolemund, G. (2016). *R for Data Science*. O'Reilly Media.
